title: SwiftUI After 7 Years: A Story of Mediocrity
excerpt: Back in 2019, SwiftUI was announced as the future of Apple development. Seven years later, it still feels like a beta version struggling with stability, performance, and many other aspects. What’s actually wrong with SwiftUI?
content_html:
Seven years after its blockbuster 2019 announcement, SwiftUI was supposed to be the mature, production-grade future of cross-platform UI development on all Apple platforms. Instead, SwiftUI feels like a perpetual beta, even in 2026. In this deep dive, I break down why the initial excitement has given way to deep professional frustration for senior engineers. I analyze the systemic issues with performance and layout predictability, the chaotic state of SwiftUI’s ever-changing data flow, and the frustrating lack of backward compatibility that forces developers into a nightmare of shims and workarounds.

Through real-world examples—including Apple’s own SwiftUI tutorial (which is broken) and a head-to-head performance comparison with UIKit (guess who wins)—I demonstrate how SwiftUI trades precise engineering for an illusion of convenience.

Beyond the code, this video explores a broader, more concerning shift in Cupertino: a transition away from the uncompromising craftsmanship of the original era of Cocoa, Aqua, and Auto Layout toward a modern corporate culture of “good enough” products. If you are tired of making excuses for broken features, fighting layout bugs, and doing Apple’s QA work for them, this perspective is for you.

Links

  • Landmarks (Apple’s broken SwiftUI tutorial)
  • Undocumented Self._printChanges() method (and other debugging tricks)
  • SwiftUI Only Makes It Easy to Develop Bad Apps
  • SwiftUI Group Still(?) Considered Harmful (another example of SwiftUI’s hidden gotchas)

Video Transcript

Intro

Okay, let’s get on with it.

This is going to be a longer piece about SwiftUI, what’s wrong with it, and why I don’t believe it’s getting better any time soon. The past seven years haven’t turned SwiftUI into a real, production-grade UI framework: It still suffers from long-standing issues with layout consistency and performance.

But you don’t have to take my word for it; you can see for yourself in Apple’s official, first-party SwiftUI tutorial. Just download the complete demo project at the link below and run it on your Mac.

I’ll get back to this particular case later in this video. But let’s start with a short retrospective.

SwiftUI was announced back in 2019—and to much fanfare. I was there and witnessed it myself. Apple promised to end the era of fighting Auto Layout and rebuilding the app every time you make the tiniest of change.

Instead, you were going to get declarative syntax, the single source of truth, built-in animation, instant previews, and cross-platform reusability of your code. To me, it sounded too good to be true.

As it turned out, it was.

By this point, the initial excitement hasn’t just faded. It’s given way to a growing sense of deep professional frustration.

And after seven years, the excuse that “SwiftUI is still a young framework,” well, it’s just dead. In this industry, seven years is like an eternity. It’s roughly the time between this and this, and it’s more than the time between the first iPhone and the iOS 7 redesign. By comparison, SwiftUI feels like it’s in a perpetual beta state. Every new feature comes with a fine-print footnote. Every layout fix breaks two more things you didn’t even touch. And honestly? I’m tired of making excuses for all this in my own projects.

Why SwiftUI Exists

But before we have a look at SwiftUI’s specific strengths and weaknesses—mostly weaknesses—let’s see why SwiftUI even exists.

It’s not so much that Apple wanted to give you great dev tools, but because it sort of had to. Apple had to respond to the pressure from the competition. By the mid-2010s, Facebook’s React became de facto standard on the web, and soon React Native and Google’s Flutter started their conquest of mobile platforms. Both frameworks are reactive and declarative.

From the perspective of any business, building native apps started to look less and less appealing. Instead, they could use the same codebase on iOS and Android while also borrowing components from their own websites.

I believe there was one more reason, and it is the Mac App Store. When was the last time you opened it? And when was the last time you installed a new native app on your Mac? Yeah, same thing here.

The iOS App Store was the key step in Apple’s transition to services business, thanks to its 30% fee on every transaction. But on the Mac, many apps only worked in the browser, or as web apps in Electron wrappers.

SwiftUI was supposed to solve both of these problems: keep developers within the native ecosystem to build new apps, and make it easier to port existing ones to the Mac.

Reactive data flows, declarative layout, and cross-platform support were the key selling points of SwiftUI. Did Apple deliver on them? Let’s have a closer look.

Data Flow

One of the biggest pain points that continues to bother senior engineers, myself included, is the data flow. On paper, the single source of truth sounds like a dream. In practice, the reality is a confusing mess of property wrappers, macros, and ever-changing supporting frameworks.

We started with @State, @Binding, and ObservedObjects. Then Apple realized the performance was disastrous and SwiftUI was re-rendering views all the time. That’s when it introduced the Observation framework and the @Observable macro. They tried to solve the problem with compiler tricks, but it clearly wasn’t enough so the layout engine continued its guessing games.

In SwiftUI, you can never know for sure how many times a view will update and, when it does, why it chose to. Even using the undocumented debugging APIs doesn’t give you the full picture.

Data flow in SwiftUI is indeed reactive—but sometimes I wish it wasn’t, because it’s reactive in all the wrong ways. It often reacts to changes it should ignore, and it ignores the changes you actually care about. To me, SwiftUI’s reactivity is a black box: It makes achieving predictable behavior almost impossible.

Layout System

That brings us to the architectural side of things. Let’s talk about SwiftUI’s layout system. If you’ve spent any time building non-trivial interfaces, you know the frustration with SwiftUI. Its layout engine is incredibly unpredictable. It is built on the idea of size negotiation, and all this sounds logical in a keynote, but it feels like a nightmare when you try to build a floating view or a custom sidebar.

And speaking of custom sidebars. That demo project from the SwiftUI tutorial has a very standard, non-custom one. You build the project with the latest Xcode and launch the app on the latest macOS—only to get this. The first time I noticed it was over two years ago, and since then, nothing has changed.

Ah, sorry, one thing has changed. Thanks to Liquid Glass, the buttons now also have different sizes—though it’s hardly a SwiftUI problem.

What is a SwiftUI problem is the overall fragility of UI layouts. They fall apart in the most unexpected ways and at the most unfortunate moments. You can see it in the very real, production apps like UTM. It’s a fantastic piece of engineering, but its reliance on SwiftUI sometimes makes it feel like an early prototype.

In the end, you find yourself wrapping everything in a GeometryReader. And this is the ultimate admission of defeat. Once you use the GeometryReader, you’ve lost the declarative benefit entirely. Now you have to calculate coordinates manually, with even more verbosity than in Auto Layout (which is ironic). And the worst thing is that you might need to rewrite all your coordinate math in the very next update, just because SwiftUI’s layout system has changed again.

API Stability & Feature Parity

Moving on to API stability and feature parity—or the lack thereof. If you look at any modern SwiftUI codebase, you’ll find it full of those if #available checks, to the point where it’s almost comical—except it’s actually embarrassing. Someone was talking about writing less code and better code, back in 2019. And what do we have seven years in?

Let’s say you want to dismiss the keyboard on scroll, the same way it worked since iOS 7. Sorry, but you need iOS 16 to do this in SwiftUI.

Okay, maybe you want to let your users customize the window toolbar, just as they could since 2001 (or something like that). Well, SwiftUI received this “breakthrough” feature only a few years ago.

And then there’s the most basic task: displaying images you fetched from the network. Well, you better write your own fetcher, because AsyncImage was introduced only in iOS 15.

But if you want to also cache those images, I’ve got bad news for you: You can’t do it at all because right now, in July 2026, this API is still in beta.

For all these scenarios, developers usually come up with their own hacks and workarounds. And when Apple finally delivers the API that existed in AppKit or UIKit for decades, you have to maintain multiple implementations.

But even if the API you use was introduced in the very first version of SwiftUI, there’s a good change it’s been renamed or replaced with a similar one. One example is the NavigationView. It was known for being super buggy. And it seems that instead of fixing it, Apple decided to replace the entire component with the NavigationStack. But this, again, means that you have to keep separate branches, for newer and older versions.

So, is that “less code” or “better code?” You tell me because I kind of don’t know.

This constant API turnover results in development hell. Instead of declaring the UI structure once, we have to write shims and patches for compatibility, and then we have to hope that they wouldn’t break apart in the next update. We’re basically doing Apple’s QA work for them.

All these problems should’ve been solved in 2019—okay, maybe 2020. Yet even after seven years, SwiftUI hasn’t achieved feature parity with the “legacy” frameworks. SwiftUI is just running around in circles, and we have to run along just to stay in the same place.

But you know what? None of this would’ve been such a big problem—but only if Apple didn’t pretend that SwiftUI is rock-solid and built for ages. This wouldn’t have been a problem if you could just write code calling the latest APIs, and then back-deploy it to older versions of iOS. Yes, you’d still have to refactor and phase out old code more frequently. But at least the current version would work consistently on all devices.

It is the way modern UI works on Android: Jetpack Compose is just a package that you get and update through a dependency manager. Then it’s simply bundled with your executable and can be used on devices as old as 2014—all while delivering the exact same UI.

Performance

Let’s talk about performance. This is where you can’t fool anyone—even though Apple still tries by only showing SwiftUI running on the latest hardware. But the fact is, SwiftUI’s performance is just not up to the standard, no matter how many times Apple has promised to improve it. It is not what I expect from a “first-class framework” running on a “premium platform.”

For example, here’s my own head-to-head comparison of UIKit and SwiftUI. The test is a simple image gallery used in the previous version of my playground app.

Why previous? Because I have since rebuilt the entire app using the ultimate cross-platform framework. But that’s a story for another time.

So, despite all the performance hacks, like decoding images on background threads, scrolling the SwiftUI grid consistently feels much less smooth. Needless to say, if you have to keep in mind some obscure optimization secrets just to make it work, all the initial simplicity of SwiftUI goes out the window.

It’s only one of the tests I performed, and I deliberately used an older iPhone for it. But it shouldn’t make any difference, because if you need an M5 Pro Max super chip just to show a bunch of JPEGs, there’s something seriously wrong with your entire architecture. That’s not how you build high-quality software; it just doesn’t work like that.

Cross-Platform Myth

This brings us to the final promise of SwiftUI—its cross-platform support. I watched a few old SwiftUI keynotes, and to be fair, I didn’t hear the words “write once, run anywhere” in any of them—it’s usually “learn those tools once, and then apply them everywhere.”

There’s but one problem. What you learned about SwiftUI on iOS is rarely applicable to layouts on the Mac. That is, unless you want to end up with UIs that feel alien, like those iPad apps that Apple brought to the Mac (yeah, these apps).

Yes, the core SwiftUI concepts, like data flow and compositional layout, are roughly the same. But the specific components you use, and the way you configure them, are often very different. Not to mention, the very same views can have inconsistent implementation across platforms.

In other words, UI design for a 6-inch phone and 27-inch desktop is not the same. Who would’ve thought?

In my experience, SwiftUI’s “learn once, apply anywhere” often turns into “learn once, learn twice, apply somewhere, debug everywhere.”

That is, of course, if you’re interested in building UIs that look native and professional. If not, SwiftUI can actually give you results that “will do” or results that are “good enough.”

Philosophical Shift

And actually, I view this “good enough” thing as the biggest problem here. I believe it serves as a sign of a major shift in Apple’s entire approach to software development. With SwiftUI, we’ve entered an era where something that “mostly works” is considered adequate. Or an era where covering only 90% of use cases is considered a success. The expectations of production-grade quality and stability gave way to so-called velocity—which is a word you use when you want to ship garbage, only do it faster.

In the days of Cocoa, that was unthinkable. In the early days of Mac OS X, that would’ve been a disaster. Can you imagine a SwiftUI version of that original Aqua keynote? Imagine for a second that instead of “liquid” buttons that look so good “you’d want to lick them,” Jobs presented flickering sidebars and jumping buttons. He would’ve been roasted.

But now, it seems that we’re settling for “good enough” products and “it will do” mentality. This is the standard of craftsmanship I’m not ready to accept.

And it’s not just a single framework issue. It’s a systemic shift. First, one company starts a trend on “moving fast and breaking things.” Gradually, more developers join it; not all of them move fast, but shipping broken things becomes normalized, even in first-party apps and system components.

For instance, Apple Music has for years had this bug where editing the queue would make the track list jump and then play an entirely wrong song.

TestFlight crops the selection with no padding.

The Settings app on the iPad shows crash reports like this, and even though I took this screenshot back in January, it hasn’t been fixed up until now.

The Home Screen shows duplicate icons for the same app. And it makes the status bar jump back and forth. And it shows outlines for icons that shouldn’t be displayed.

And even professional apps like Logic Pro now ship with missing localization. You know, those professional apps that are supposed to be the benchmark of quality and stability.

I can go on for a long time.

While not all of these examples use SwiftUI, they demonstrate the level of quality that Apple considers “acceptable” now. I didn’t have to dig deep to find them; these are the things that I personally saw in the past few months.

So with these examples in mind, it’s not surprising that the flagship system framework makes it nearly impossible to build an app that’s not broken in at least one way.

On Apple platforms in particular, this shift began around 2018, with those “alien” apps I already mentioned. It’s when Project Marzipan, later renamed Catalyst, first enabled UIKit code to be reused on the Mac. Tech reviewers tore apart the results, and here’s more screenshots.

But instead of doing the homework, Apple doubled-down on the idea of cross-platform development, with SwiftUI. And this brand-new, completely untested framework only introduced more issues with performance, stability, and visual appeal.

I conclude that lowering the bar for quality was a choice, not a necessity. I refuse to accept that choice. And that is why I can’t trust SwiftUI even after seven years.

Summary

As a bottom line, and to answer the question from the beginning, what is actually wrong with SwiftUI?

If you weigh in all the problems that haven’t been fixed in the seven years of its existence, the answer is,

Everything.

Or at least everything that’s important for building stable, performant, and maintainable systems.

The story of SwiftUI is a story of mediocrity and falling standards. We’re offered to trade predictable precision for an illusion of convenience. And then we’re forced to either spend the time debugging the framework, or ship broken apps as is.

As a senior engineer, I find neither of these options appealing. I don’t respect the “it will do” mindset, and I believe that users deserve better than “good enough.”

SwiftUI is not truly bad. It’s mediocre. And that, in my opinion, is much, much worse.

So for now, I still prefer the “legacy” UI frameworks.

Afterthought

The idea of this piece came to me even before I started this channel. For years, I’ve been observing SwiftUI’s struggle to become a solid replacement for AppKit and UIKit—in other words, to become what Apple promised it to be, all the way back in 2019.

For years, I’ve been testing SwiftUI’s new iterations in the hopes that the problems that plague it will finally get fixed.

But as the time goes by, SwiftUI’s not becoming better in a fundamental way. It’s just as half-baked as it was seven years ago, and apps built with SwiftUI mostly turn out just as unremarkable.

But SwiftUI’s struggle is not the only thing I’ve been observing. I’ve also been observing software engineers who sincerely believed that if a feature built with SwiftUI works right here and right now, then their job is done. Unless they choose the inferior tools on purpose, I don’t really blame them.

Well, maybe a little, because you can’t ignore the long-term cost of maintenance without paying the price.

Anyway, individual engineers aren’t usually the ones who pay it; their employers are. But in the times when businesses are obsessed with replacing humans with AI agents, it’s hard to expect the quality of their products to improve. And because these are also the same businesses that view software development as a commodity or linear production, they typically want to ship “fast” instead of “right.” We can already see the results of this approach, and we’re going to see more in the future.

Outro

That’s it for today’s Code Bird video, but I am very interested in your opinion, especially if you disagree with me. I would love to read your comments down below.

Give this video a thumbs-up if you feel it deserves one. Subscribe to the channel for more engineering content.

I’ll see you in the next video. Until then, make your tools fly.

I didn’t have to dig deep to find them; these are the things that I personally saw in the past few months. So with these examples in mind, it’s not surprising that the flagship system framework makes it nearly impossible to build an app that’s not broken in at least one way. On Apple platforms in particular, this shift began around 2018, with those “alien” apps I already mentioned. It’s when Project Marzipan, later renamed Catalyst, first enabled UIKit code to be reused on the Mac. Tech reviewers tore apart the results, and here’s more screenshots. But instead of doing the homework, Apple doubled-down on the idea of cross-platform development, with SwiftUI. And this brand-new, completely untested framework only introduced more issues with performance, stability, and visual appeal. I conclude that lowering the bar for quality was a choice, not a necessity. I refuse to accept that choice. And that is why I can’t trust SwiftUI even after seven years. Summary As a bottom line, and to answer the question from the beginning, what is actually wrong with SwiftUI? If you weigh in all the problems that haven’t been fixed in the seven years of its existence, the answer is, Everything. Or at least everything that’s important for building stable, performant, and maintainable systems. The story of SwiftUI is a story of mediocrity and falling standards. We’re offered to trade predictable precision for an illusion of convenience. And then we’re forced to either spend the time debugging the framework, or ship broken apps as is. As a senior engineer, I find neither of these options appealing. I don’t respect the “it will do” mindset, and I believe that users deserve better than “good enough.” SwiftUI is not truly bad. It’s mediocre. And that, in my opinion, is much, much worse. So for now, I still prefer the “legacy” UI frameworks. Afterthought The idea of this piece came to me even before I started this channel. For years, I’ve been observing SwiftUI’s struggle to become a solid replacement for AppKit and UIKit—in other words, to become what Apple promised it to be, all the way back in 2019. For years, I’ve been testing SwiftUI’s new iterations in the hopes that the problems that plague it will finally get fixed. But as the time goes by, SwiftUI’s not becoming better in a fundamental way. It’s just as half-baked as it was seven years ago, and apps built with SwiftUI mostly turn out just as unremarkable. But SwiftUI’s struggle is not the only thing I’ve been observing. I’ve also been observing software engineers who sincerely believed that if a feature built with SwiftUI works right here and right now, then their job is done. Unless they choose the inferior tools on purpose, I don’t really blame them. Well, maybe a little, because you can’t ignore the long-term cost of maintenance without paying the price. Anyway, individual engineers aren’t usually the ones who pay it; their employers are. But in the times when businesses are obsessed with replacing humans with AI agents, it’s hard to expect the quality of their products to improve. And because these are also the same businesses that view software development as a commodity or linear production, they typically want to ship “fast” instead of “right.” We can already see the results of this approach, and we’re going to see more in the future. Outro That’s it for today’s Code Bird video, but I am very interested in your opinion, especially if you disagree with me. I would love to read your comments down below. Give this video a thumbs-up if you feel it deserves one. Subscribe to the channel for more engineering content. I’ll see you in the next video. Until then, make your tools fly.

blocks.html_en: API Stability & Feature Parity

sentences.en: API Stability & Feature Parity
sentences.zh: API 稳定性和功能对等

blocks.html_en: Moving on to API stability and feature parity—or the lack thereof. sentences.en: Moving on to API stability and feature parity—or the lack thereof.
sentences.zh: 接下来讨论 API 稳定性和功能对等性——或者说缺乏这些。

sentences.en: If you look at any modern SwiftUI codebase, you’ll find it full of those if #available checks, to the point where it’s almost comical—except it’s actually embarrassing.
sentences.zh: 如果你查看任何现代 SwiftUI 代码库，你会发现它充满了 if #available 检查，几乎到了滑稽的地步——只不过它实际上很尴尬。

sentences.en: Someone was talking about writing less code and better code, back in 2019.
sentences.zh: 早在 2019 年，就有人在谈论编写更少的代码和更好的代码。

sentences.en: And what do we have seven years in?
sentences.zh: 那么我们的七年时间是什么呢？

blocks.html_en: Let’s say you want to dismiss the keyboard on scroll, the same way it worked since iOS 7. Sorry, but you need iOS 16 to do this in SwiftUI.

sentences.en: Let’s say you want to dismiss the keyboard on scroll, the same way it worked since iOS 7.
sentences.zh: 假设您想在滚动时关闭键盘，就像 iOS 7 以来的工作方式一样。

sentences.en: Sorry, but you need iOS 16 to do this in SwiftUI.
sentences.zh: 抱歉，您需要 iOS 16 才能在 SwiftUI 中执行此操作。

blocks.html_en: Okay, maybe you want to let your users customize the window toolbar, just as they could since 2001 (or something like that). Well, SwiftUI received this “breakthrough” feature only a few years ago.

sentences.en: Okay, maybe you want to let your users customize the window toolbar, just as they could since 2001 (or something like that).
sentences.zh: 好吧，也许您想让您的用户自定义窗口工具栏，就像他们自 2001 年以来所做的那样（或类似的事情）。

sentences.en: Well, SwiftUI received this “breakthrough” feature only a few years ago.
sentences.zh: 嗯，SwiftUI 仅仅在几年前就获得了这个“突破性”功能。

blocks.html_en: And then there’s the most basic task: displaying images you fetched from the network. Well, you better write your own fetcher, because AsyncImage was introduced only in iOS 15.

sentences.en: And then there’s the most basic task: displaying images you fetched from the network.
sentences.zh: 然后是最基本的任务：显示从网络获取的图像。

sentences.en: Well, you better write your own fetcher, because AsyncImage was introduced only in iOS 15.
sentences.zh: 好吧，你最好编写自己的 fetcher，因为 AsyncImage 仅在 iOS 15 中引入。

blocks.html_en: But if you want to also cache those images, I’ve got bad news for you: You can’t do it at all because right now, in July 2026, this API is still in beta.

sentences.en: But if you want to also cache those images, I’ve got bad news for you: You can’t do it at all because right now, in July 2026, this API is still in beta.
sentences.zh: 但如果您还想缓存这些图像，我有一个坏消息要告诉您：您根本无法做到这一点，因为现在，即 2026 年 7 月，该 API 仍处于测试阶段。

blocks.html_en: For all these scenarios, developers usually come up with their own hacks and workarounds. And when Apple finally delivers the API that existed in AppKit or UIKit for decades, you have to maintain multiple implementations.

sentences.en: For all these scenarios, developers usually come up with their own hacks and workarounds.
sentences.zh: 对于所有这些场景，开发人员通常会想出自己的技巧和解决方法。

sentences.en: And when Apple finally delivers the API that existed in AppKit or UIKit for decades, you have to maintain multiple implementations.
sentences.zh: 当 Apple 最终提供 AppKit 或 UIKit 中存在了数十年的 API 时，您必须维护多个实现。

blocks.html_en: But even if the API you use was introduced in the very first version of SwiftUI, there’s a good change it’s been renamed or replaced with a similar one. sentences.en: But even if the API you use was introduced in the very first version of SwiftUI, there’s a good change it’s been renamed or replaced with a similar one.
sentences.zh: 但即使您使用的 API 是在 SwiftUI 的第一个版本中引入的，也有一个很好的变化，它已被重命名或替换为类似的 API。

sentences.en: One example is the NavigationView.
sentences.zh: 导航视图就是一个例子。

sentences.en: It was known for being super buggy.
sentences.zh: 它以超级越野车而闻名。

sentences.en: And it seems that instead of fixing it, Apple decided to replace the entire component with the NavigationStack.
sentences.zh: 看起来苹果并没有修复它，而是决定用 NavigationStack 替换整个组件。

sentences.en: But this, again, means that you have to keep separate branches, for newer and older versions.
sentences.zh: 但这又意味着您必须为新版本和旧版本保留单独的分支。

blocks.html_en: So, is that “less code” or “better code?” You tell me because I kind of don’t know.

sentences.en: So, is that “less code” or “better code?”
sentences.zh: 那么，这是“更少的代码”还是“更好的代码”？

sentences.en: You tell me because I kind of don’t know.
sentences.zh: 你告诉我，因为我有点不知道。

blocks.html_en: This constant API turnover results in development hell. Instead of declaring the UI structure once, we have to write shims and patches for compatibility, and then we have to hope that they wouldn’t break apart in the next update. We’re basically doing Apple’s QA work for them.

sentences.en: This constant API turnover results in development hell.
sentences.zh: 这种持续的 API 更新导致了开发地狱。

sentences.en: Instead of declaring the UI structure once, we have to write shims and patches for compatibility, and then we have to hope that they wouldn’t break apart in the next update.
sentences.zh: 我们不必一次性声明 UI 结构，而是必须编写填充程序和补丁来实现兼容性，然后我们必须希望它们不会在下一次更新中崩溃。

sentences.en: We’re basically doing Apple’s QA work for them.
sentences.zh: 我们基本上是在为他们做苹果的质量保证工作。

blocks.html_en: All these problems should’ve been solved in 2019—okay, maybe 2020. Yet even after seven years, SwiftUI hasn’t achieved feature parity with the “legacy” frameworks. SwiftUI is just running around in circles, and we have to run along just to stay in the same place.

sentences.en: All these problems should’ve been solved in 2019—okay, maybe 2020.
sentences.zh: 所有这些问题都应该在 2019 年得到解决——好吧，也许是 2020 年。

sentences.en: Yet even after seven years, SwiftUI hasn’t achieved feature parity with the “legacy” frameworks.
sentences.zh: 然而，即使七年过去了，SwiftUI 仍未实现与“传统”框架同等的功能。

sentences.en: SwiftUI is just running around in circles, and we have to run along just to stay in the same place.
sentences.zh: SwiftUI 只是在原地打转，而我们必须一直跑才能留在同一个地方。

blocks.html_en: But you know what? None of this would’ve been such a big problem—but only if Apple didn’t pretend that SwiftUI is rock-solid and built for ages. sentences.en: But you know what?
sentences.zh: 但你知道吗？

sentences.en: None of this would’ve been such a big problem—but only if Apple didn’t pretend that SwiftUI is rock-solid and built for ages.
sentences.zh: 这一切都不会是一个大问题——但前提是苹果不假装 SwiftUI 坚如磐石并且已经建立了很多年。

sentences.en: This wouldn’t have been a problem if you could just write code calling the latest APIs, and then back-deploy it to older versions of iOS.
sentences.zh: 如果您只需编写调用最新 API 的代码，然后将其反向部署到旧版本的 iOS，那么这就不成问题了。

sentences.en: Yes, you’d still have to refactor and phase out old code more frequently.
sentences.zh: 是的，您仍然需要更频繁地重构和逐步淘汰旧代码。

sentences.en: But at least the current version would work consistently on all devices.
sentences.zh: 但至少当前版本可以在所有设备上一致运行。

blocks.html_en: It is the way modern UI works on Android: Jetpack Compose is just a package that you get and update through a dependency manager. Then it’s simply bundled with your executable and can be used on devices as old as 2014—all while delivering the exact same UI.

sentences.en: It is the way modern UI works on Android: Jetpack Compose is just a package that you get and update through a dependency manager.
sentences.zh: 这是现代 UI 在 Android 上的工作方式：Jetpack Compose 只是您通过依赖项管理器获取和更新的包。

sentences.en: Then it’s simply bundled with your executable and can be used on devices as old as 2014—all while delivering the exact same UI.
sentences.zh: 然后，它只需与您的可执行文件捆绑在一起，即可在 2014 年以前的设备上使用，同时提供完全相同的 UI。

blocks.html_en: Performance

sentences.en: Performance
sentences.zh: 表现

blocks.html_en: Let’s talk about performance. This is where you can’t fool anyone—even though Apple still tries by only showing SwiftUI running on the latest hardware. But the fact is, SwiftUI’s performance is just not up to the standard, no matter how many times Apple has promised to improve it. sentences.en: Let’s talk about performance.
sentences.zh: 我们来谈谈性能。

sentences.en: This is where you can’t fool anyone—even though Apple still tries by only showing SwiftUI running on the latest hardware.
sentences.zh: 这是你无法愚弄任何人的地方——尽管苹果仍然尝试只显示在最新硬件上运行的 SwiftUI。

sentences.en: But the fact is, SwiftUI’s performance is just not up to the standard, no matter how many times Apple has promised to improve it.

sentences.zh: 该测试是我的游乐场应用程序的早期版本中使用的简单图片库。

blocks.html_en: Why previous? Because I have since rebuilt the entire app using the ultimate cross-platform framework. But that’s a story for another time.

sentences.en: Why previous?
sentences.zh: 为什么是以前的？

sentences.en: Because I have since rebuilt the entire app using the ultimate cross-platform framework.
sentences.zh: 因为我已经使用终极跨平台框架重建了整个应用程序。

sentences.en: But that’s a story for another time.
sentences.zh: 但这是另一个故事了。

blocks.html_en: So, despite all the performance hacks, like decoding images on background threads, scrolling the SwiftUI grid consistently feels much less smooth. sentences.en: So, despite all the performance hacks, like decoding images on background threads, scrolling the SwiftUI grid consistently feels much less smooth.
sentences.zh: 因此，尽管有所有的性能改进，比如在后台线程上解码图像，滚动 SwiftUI 网格始终感觉不太流畅。

sentences.en: Needless to say, if you have to keep in mind some obscure optimization secrets just to make it work, all the initial simplicity of SwiftUI goes out the window.
sentences.zh: 不用说，如果您必须牢记一些晦涩的优化秘密才能使其正常工作，那么 SwiftUI 最初的所有简单性都会消失。

blocks.html_en: It’s only one of the tests I performed, and I deliberately used an older iPhone for it. sentences.en: It’s only one of the tests I performed, and I deliberately used an older iPhone for it.
sentences.zh: 这只是我进行的测试之一，我特意使用了旧款 iPhone 来进行测试。

sentences.en: But it shouldn’t make any difference, because if you need an M5 Pro Max super chip just to show a bunch of JPEGs, there’s something seriously wrong with your entire architecture.

sentences.en: That’s not how you build high-quality software; it just doesn’t work like that.

blocks.html_en: Cross-Platform Myth

sentences.en: Cross-Platform Myth
sentences.zh: 跨平台神话

blocks.html_en: This brings us to the final promise of SwiftUI—its cross-platform support. I watched a few old SwiftUI keynotes, and to be fair, I didn’t hear the words “write once, run anywhere” in any of them—it’s usually “learn those tools once, and then apply them everywhere.”

sentences.en: This brings us to the final promise of SwiftUI—its cross-platform support.
sentences.zh: 这给我们带来了 SwiftUI 的最终承诺——跨平台支持。

sentences.en: I watched a few old SwiftUI keynotes, and to be fair, I didn’t hear the words “write once, run anywhere” in any of them—it’s usually “learn those tools once, and then apply them everywhere.”
sentences.zh: 我观看了一些旧的 SwiftUI 主题演讲，公平地说，我没有在其中任何一个中听到“一次编写，随处运行”这句话 - 通常是“学习这些工具一次，然后在任何地方应用它们”。

blocks.html_en: There’s but one problem. What you learned about SwiftUI on iOS is rarely applicable to layouts on the Mac. That is, unless you want to end up with UIs that feel alien, like those iPad apps that Apple brought to the Mac (yeah, these apps).

sentences.en: There’s but one problem.
sentences.zh: 只有一个问题。

sentences.en: What you learned about SwiftUI on iOS is rarely applicable to layouts on the Mac.
sentences.zh: 您在 iOS 上学到的有关 SwiftUI 的知识很少适用于 Mac 上的布局。

sentences.en: That is, unless you want to end up with UIs that feel alien, like those iPad apps that Apple brought to the Mac (yeah, these apps).
sentences.zh: 也就是说，除非你想最终得到感觉陌生的 UI，就像 Apple 带到 Mac 上的那些 iPad 应用程序（是的，这些应用程序）。

blocks.html_en: Yes, the core SwiftUI concepts, like data flow and compositional layout, are roughly the same. But the specific components you use, and the way you configure them, are often very different. Not to mention, the very same views can have inconsistent implementation across platforms.

sentences.en: Yes, the core SwiftUI concepts, like data flow and compositional layout, are roughly the same.
sentences.zh: 是的，核心 SwiftUI 概念（例如数据流和组合布局）大致相同。

sentences.en: But the specific components you use, and the way you configure them, are often very different.
sentences.zh: 但您使用的具体组件以及配置它们的方式通常非常不同。

sentences.en: Not to mention, the very same views can have inconsistent implementation across platforms.
sentences.zh: 更不用说，相同的视图在不同平台上的实现可能会不一致。

blocks.html_en: In other words, UI design for a 6-inch phone and 27-inch desktop is not the same. Who would’ve thought?

sentences.en: In other words, UI design for a 6-inch phone and 27-inch desktop is not the same.
sentences.zh: 也就是说，6英寸手机和27英寸台式机的UI设计是不一样的。

sentences.en: Who would’ve thought?

blocks.html_en: In my experience, SwiftUI’s “learn once, apply anywhere” often turns into “learn once, learn twice, apply somewhere, debug everywhere.”

sentences.en: In my experience, SwiftUI’s “learn once, apply anywhere” often turns into “learn once, learn twice, apply somewhere, debug everywhere.”
sentences.zh: 根据我的经验，SwiftUI 的“学习一次，在任何地方应用”通常会变成“学习一次，学习两次，在任何地方应用，在任何地方调试”。

blocks.html_en: That is, of course, if you’re interested in building UIs that look native and professional. If not, SwiftUI can actually give you results that “will do” or results that are “good enough.”

blocks.html_en: Philosophical Shift

sentences.en: Philosophical Shift
sentences.zh: 哲学转变

blocks.html_en: And actually, I view this “good enough” thing as the biggest problem here. I believe it serves as a sign of a major shift in Apple’s entire approach to software development. sentences.en: And actually, I view this “good enough” thing as the biggest problem here.
sentences.zh: 事实上，我认为“足够好”是这里最大的问题。

sentences.en: I believe it serves as a sign of a major shift in Apple’s entire approach to software development.
sentences.zh: 我相信这是苹果整个软件开发方法发生重大转变的标志。

sentences.en: With SwiftUI, we’ve entered an era where something that “mostly works” is considered adequate.
sentences.zh: 有了 SwiftUI，我们已经进入了一个“大部分有效”的东西就被认为足够的时代。

sentences.en: Or an era where covering only 90% of use cases is considered a success.
sentences.zh: 或者说只覆盖90%的用例就算成功的时代。

sentences.en: The expectations of production-grade quality and stability gave way to so-called velocity—which is a word you use when you want to ship garbage, only do it faster.
sentences.zh: 对生产级质量和稳定性的期望让位于所谓的速度——当你想要运送垃圾时，你会使用这个词，只是做得更快。

blocks.html_en: In the days of Cocoa, that was unthinkable. In the early days of Mac OS X, that would’ve been a disaster. Can you imagine a SwiftUI version of that original Aqua keynote? sentences.en: In the days of Cocoa, that was unthinkable.
sentences.zh: 在可可时代，这是不可想象的。

sentences.en: In the early days of Mac OS X, that would’ve been a disaster.
sentences.zh: 在 Mac OS X 的早期，这将是一场灾难。

sentences.en: Can you imagine a SwiftUI version of that original Aqua keynote?
sentences.zh: 您能想象原始 Aqua 主题演讲的 SwiftUI 版本吗？

sentences.en: Imagine for a second that instead of “liquid” buttons that look so good “you’d want to lick them,” Jobs presented flickering sidebars and jumping buttons.
sentences.zh: 想象一下，乔布斯展示的不是那些看起来很棒“你会想舔它们”的“液体”按钮，而是闪烁的侧边栏和跳跃按钮。

sentences.en: He would’ve been roasted.
sentences.zh: 他会被烤死的。

blocks.html_en: But now, it seems that we’re settling for “good enough” products and “it will do” mentality. This is the standard of craftsmanship I’m not ready to accept.

sentences.en: But now, it seems that we’re settling for “good enough” products and “it will do” mentality.
sentences.zh: 但现在，我们似乎满足于“足够好”的产品和“它会做”的心态。

sentences.en: This is the standard of craftsmanship I’m not ready to accept.
sentences.zh: 这是我不准备接受的工艺标准。

blocks.html_en: And it’s not just a single framework issue. It’s a systemic shift. sentences.en: And it’s not just a single framework issue.
sentences.zh: 这不仅仅是一个单一的框架问题。

sentences.en: It’s a systemic shift.
sentences.zh: 这是一个系统性的转变。

sentences.en: First, one company starts a trend on “moving fast and breaking things.”
sentences.zh: 首先，一家公司开创了一种“快速行动、打破常规”的趋势。

sentences.en: Gradually, more developers join it; not all of them move fast, but shipping broken things becomes normalized, even in first-party apps and system components.
sentences.zh: 渐渐地，更多的开发者加入其中；并非所有的移动速度都很快，但运送损坏的东西变得常态化，即使在第一方应用程序和系统组件中也是如此。

blocks.html_en: For instance, Apple Music has for years had this bug where editing the queue would make the track list jump and then play an entirely wrong song.

content_html_zh:
在 2019 年发布轰动一时的 7 年后，SwiftUI 被认为是所有 Apple 平台上跨平台 UI 开发的成熟、生产级的未来。 相反，SwiftUI 给人的感觉就像是一个永久的测试版，即使是在 2026 年。 在这次深入探讨中，我分析了为什么高级工程师最初的兴奋已经让位于深深的职业挫败感。 我分析了性能和布局可预测性方面的系统性问题、SwiftUI 不断变化的数据流的混乱状态，以及令人沮丧的缺乏向后兼容性，迫使开发人员陷入垫片和解决方法的噩梦。

通过现实世界的例子——包括苹果自己的 SwiftUI 教程（已损坏）以及与 UIKit 的头对头性能比较（猜猜谁赢了）——我演示了 SwiftUI 如何用精确的工程换取便利的幻觉。

除了代码之外，该视频还探讨了库比蒂诺更广泛、更令人担忧的转变：从 Cocoa、Aqua 和 Auto Layout 原始时代毫不妥协的工艺转向“足够好”产品的现代企业文化。 如果您厌倦了为功能损坏找借口、与布局错误作斗争以及为它们做 Apple 的 QA 工作，那么这个观点适合您。

Links

  • Landmarks（Apple 损坏的 SwiftUI 教程）
  • 未记录的 Self._printChanges() 方法（以及其他调试技巧）
  • SwiftUI 只会让开发糟糕的应用程序变得容易
  • SwiftUI 组仍然（？） 被认为是有害的（SwiftUI 隐藏陷阱的另一个例子）

视频文字记录

Intro

好吧，让我们继续吧。

这将是一篇关于 SwiftUI 的较长文章，它有什么问题，以及为什么我不相信它会很快变得更好。 过去七年并没有将 SwiftUI 变成真正的生产级 UI 框架：它仍然面临布局一致性和性能方面长期存在的问题。

但你不必相信我的话；您可以在 Apple 官方的第一方 SwiftUI 教程中亲自查看。 只需从下面的链接下载完整的演示项目并在您的 Mac 上运行即可。

我将在本视频稍后部分讨论这个特殊案例。 但让我们从一个简短的回顾开始。

SwiftUI 早在 2019 年就宣布了，并且引起了很大的关注。 我当时就在场，亲眼目睹了这一幕。 苹果承诺结束与自动布局作斗争并在每次做出最微小的更改时重建应用程序的时代。

相反，您将获得声明性语法、单一事实来源、内置动画、即时预览以及代码的跨平台可重用性。 对我来说，这听起来好得令人难以置信。

事实证明，确实如此。

至此，最初的兴奋还没有消退。 它已经被一种日益强烈的职业挫败感所取代。

七年后，“SwiftUI 仍然是一个年轻框架”的借口，好吧，它已经死了。 在这个行业，七年就像一个世纪。 这大约是这个和这个之间的时间，并且比第一代 iPhone 和 iOS 7 重新设计之间的时间还要长。 相比之下，SwiftUI 感觉就像处于永久测试状态。 每个新功能都带有精美的脚注。 每一次布局修复都会破坏另外两个你甚至没有碰过的东西。 老实说？ 我厌倦了在自己的项目中为这一切找借口。

为什么 SwiftUI 存在

但在我们了解 SwiftUI 的具体优点和缺点（主要是缺点）之前，让我们先看看 SwiftUI 存在的原因。

苹果并不是想为你提供出色的开发工具，而是因为它不得不这样做。 苹果必须应对来自竞争的压力。 到 2010 年代中期，Facebook 的 React 成为事实上的网络标准，很快 React Native 和 Google 的 Flutter 开始征服移动平台。 这两个框架都是响应式和声明式的。

从任何企业的角度来看，构建原生应用程序开始看起来越来越没有吸引力。 相反，他们可以在 iOS 和 Android 上使用相同的代码库，同时还可以从自己的网站借用组件。

我相信还有一个原因，那就是 Mac App Store。 您最后一次打开它是什么时候？ 您最后一次在 Mac 上安装新的本机应用程序是什么时候？ 是的，这里也一样。

iOS App Store 是苹果向服务业务转型的关键一步，它对每笔交易收取 30% 的费用。 但在 Mac 上，许多应用程序只能在浏览器中运行，或者作为 Electron 包装器中的 Web 应用程序运行。

SwiftUI 本来应该解决这两个问题：让开发人员在原生生态系统中构建新​​应用程序，并使现有应用程序更容易移植到 Mac。

响应式数据流、声明式布局和跨平台支持是 SwiftUI 的主要卖点。 苹果兑现了这些承诺吗？ 让我们仔细看看。

数据流

持续困扰高级工程师（包括我自己）的最大痛点之一是数据流。 从纸面上看，单一事实来源听起来就像一个梦想。 在实践中，现实是由属性包装器、宏和不断变化的支持框架组成的混乱混乱。

我们从@State、@Binding 和ObservedObjects 开始。 然后苹果意识到性能是灾难性的，SwiftUI 一直在重新渲染视图。 就在那时，它引入了 Observation 框架和 @Observable 宏。 他们试图用编译器技巧来解决这个问题，但这显然还不够，因此布局引擎继续进行猜谜游戏。

在 SwiftUI 中，您永远无法确定视图将更新多少次，以及更新时的原因。 即使使用未记录的调试 API 也无法让您了解全部情况。

SwiftUI 中的数据流确实是响应式的，但有时我希望它不是，因为它以所有错误的方式进行响应。 它通常会对它应该忽略的更改做出反应，并且它会忽略您真正关心的更改。 对我来说，SwiftUI 的反应性是一个黑匣子：它使得实现可预测的行为几乎不可能。

布局系统

这将我们带到了建筑方面。 我们来谈谈 SwiftUI 的布局系统。 如果您花过时间构建重要的界面，您就会知道 SwiftUI 的挫败感。 它的布局引擎是非常难以预测的。 它建立在尺寸协商的理念之上，所有这些在主题演讲中听起来都很合乎逻辑，但当您尝试构建浮动视图或自定义侧边栏时，感觉就像一场噩梦。

说到自定义侧边栏。 SwiftUI 教程中的演示项目有一个非常标准的非自定义项目。 您使用最新的 Xcode 构建项目并在最新的 macOS 上启动应用程序 - 只是为了得到这个。 我第一次注意到它是在两年多前，从那时起，一切都没有改变。

啊，抱歉，有一件事发生了变化。 多亏了 Liquid Glass，按钮现在也有了不同的尺寸——尽管这并不是 SwiftUI 的问题。

SwiftUI 的问题在于 UI 布局的整体脆弱性。 他们以最意想不到的方式和最不幸的时刻崩溃了。 您可以在 UTM 等非常真实的生产应用程序中看到它。 这是一个非常棒的工程，但它对 SwiftUI 的依赖有时让它感觉像是一个早期的原型。

最后，您发现自己将所有内容都包装在 GeometryReader 中。 这就是最终的承认失败。 一旦使用 GeometryReader，您就完全失去了声明性的好处。 现在您必须手动计算坐标，比自动布局更加冗长（这很讽刺）。 最糟糕的是，您可能需要在下一次更新中重写所有坐标数学，只是因为 SwiftUI 的布局系统再次发生了变化。

API 稳定性和功能对等

接下来讨论 API 稳定性和功能对等性——或者说缺乏这些。 如果你查看任何现代 SwiftUI 代码库，你会发现它充满了 if #available 检查，几乎到了滑稽的地步——只不过它实际上很尴尬。 早在 2019 年，就有人在谈论编写更少的代码和更好的代码。 那么我们的七年时间是什么呢？

假设您想在滚动时关闭键盘，就像 iOS 7 以来的工作方式一样。 抱歉，您需要 iOS 16 才能在 SwiftUI 中执行此操作。

好吧，也许您想让您的用户自定义窗口工具栏，就像他们自 2001 年以来所做的那样（或类似的事情）。 嗯，SwiftUI 仅仅在几年前就获得了这个“突破性”功能。

然后是最基本的任务：显示从网络获取的图像。 好吧，你最好编写自己的 fetcher，因为 AsyncImage 仅在 iOS 15 中引入。

但如果您还想缓存这些图像，我有一个坏消息要告诉您：您根本无法做到这一点，因为现在，即 2026 年 7 月，该 API 仍处于测试阶段。

对于所有这些场景，开发人员通常会想出自己的技巧和解决方法。 当 Apple 最终提供 AppKit 或 UIKit 中存在了数十年的 API 时，您必须维护多个实现。

但即使您使用的 API 是在 SwiftUI 的第一个版本中引入的，也有一个很好的变化，它已被重命名或替换为类似的 API。 导航视图就是一个例子。 它以超级越野车而闻名。 看起来苹果并没有修复它，而是决定用 NavigationStack 替换整个组件。 但这又意味着您必须为新版本和旧版本保留单独的分支。

那么，这是“更少的代码”还是“更好的代码”？ 你告诉我，因为我有点不知道。

这种持续的 API 更新导致了开发地狱。 我们不必一次性声明 UI 结构，而是必须编写填充程序和补丁来实现兼容性，然后我们必须希望它们不会在下一次更新中崩溃。 我们基本上是在为他们做苹果的质量保证工作。

所有这些问题都应该在 2019 年得到解决——好吧，也许是 2020 年。 然而，即使七年过去了，SwiftUI 仍未实现与“传统”框架同等的功能。 SwiftUI 只是在原地打转，而我们必须一直跑才能留在同一个地方。

但你知道吗？ 这一切都不会是一个大问题——但前提是苹果不假装 SwiftUI 坚如磐石并且已经建立了很多年。 如果您只需编写调用最新 API 的代码，然后将其反向部署到旧版本的 iOS，那么这就不成问题了。 是的，您仍然需要更频繁地重构和逐步淘汰旧代码。 但至少当前版本可以在所有设备上一致运行。

这是现代 UI 在 Android 上的工作方式：Jetpack Compose 只是您通过依赖项管理器获取和更新的包。 然后，它只需与您的可执行文件捆绑在一起，即可在 2014 年以前的设备上使用，同时提供完全相同的 UI。

表现

我们来谈谈性能。 这是你无法愚弄任何人的地方——尽管苹果仍然尝试只显示在最新硬件上运行的 SwiftUI。 但事实是，无论苹果承诺多少次改进，SwiftUI 的性能仍然达不到标准。 这不是我对在“高级平台”上运行的“一流框架”的期望。

例如，这是我自己对 UIKit 和 SwiftUI 的头对头比较。 该测试是我的游乐场应用程序的早期版本中使用的简单图片库。

为什么是以前的？ 因为我已经使用终极跨平台框架重建了整个应用程序。 但这是另一个故事了。

因此，尽管有所有的性能改进，比如在后台线程上解码图像，滚动 SwiftUI 网格始终感觉不太流畅。 不用说，如果您必须牢记一些晦涩的优化秘密才能使其正常工作，那么 SwiftUI 最初的所有简单性都会消失。

这只是我进行的测试之一，我特意使用了旧款 iPhone 来进行测试。 但这应该没有什么区别，因为如果你需要 M5 Pro Max 超级芯片只是为了显示一堆 JPEG，那么你的整个架构就存在严重问题。 这不是构建高质量软件的方式。但事实并非如此。

跨平台神话

这给我们带来了 SwiftUI 的最终承诺——跨平台支持。 我观看了一些旧的 SwiftUI 主题演讲，公平地说，我没有在其中任何一个中听到“一次编写，随处运行”这句话 - 通常是“学习这些工具一次，然后在任何地方应用它们”。

只有一个问题。 您在 iOS 上学到的有关 SwiftUI 的知识很少适用于 Mac 上的布局。 也就是说，除非你想最终得到感觉陌生的 UI，就像 Apple 带到 Mac 上的那些 iPad 应用程序（是的，这些应用程序）。

是的，核心 SwiftUI 概念（例如数据流和组合布局）大致相同。 但您使用的具体组件以及配置它们的方式通常非常不同。 更不用说，相同的视图在不同平台上的实现可能会不一致。

也就是说，6英寸手机和27英寸台式机的UI设计是不一样的。 谁会想到呢？

根据我的经验，SwiftUI 的“学习一次，在任何地方应用”通常会变成“学习一次，学习两次，在任何地方应用，在任何地方调试”。

当然，如果您有兴趣构建看起来原生且专业的用户界面。 如果没有，SwiftUI 实际上可以给你“可以”的结果或“足够好”的结果。

哲学转变

事实上，我认为“足够好”是这里最大的问题。 我相信这是苹果整个软件开发方法发生重大转变的标志。 有了 SwiftUI，我们已经进入了一个“大部分有效”的东西就被认为足够的时代。 或者说只覆盖90%的用例就算成功的时代。 对生产级质量和稳定性的期望让位于所谓的速度——当你想要运送垃圾时，你会使用这个词，只是做得更快。

在可可时代，这是不可想象的。 在 Mac OS X 的早期，这将是一场灾难。 您能想象原始 Aqua 主题演讲的 SwiftUI 版本吗？ 想象一下，乔布斯展示的不是那些看起来很棒“你会想舔它们”的“液体”按钮，而是闪烁的侧边栏和跳跃按钮。 他会被烤死的。

但现在，我们似乎满足于“足够好”的产品和“它会做”的心态。 这是我不准备接受的工艺标准。

这不仅仅是一个单一的框架问题。 这是一个系统性的转变。 首先，一家公司开创了一种“快速行动、打破常规”的趋势。 渐渐地，更多的开发者加入其中；并非所有的移动速度都很快，但运送损坏的东西变得常态化，即使在第一方应用程序和系统组件中也是如此。

例如，Apple Music 多年来一直存在这样的错误：编辑队列会使曲目列表跳转，然后播放完全错误的歌曲。

TestFlight 裁剪选区，没有填充。

iPad 上的“设置”应用程序显示了这样的崩溃报告，尽管我在一月份截取了这张屏幕截图，但直到现在它还没有得到修复。

主屏幕显示同一应用程序的重复图标。 并且它使状态栏来回跳跃。 它还显示不应显示的图标的轮廓。

甚至像 Logic Pro 这样的专业应用程序现在也缺少本地化。 要知道，那些专业的应用程序应该是质量和稳定性的基准。

我可以继续很长一段时间。

虽然并非所有这些示例都使用 SwiftUI，但它们展示了 Apple 目前认为“可接受”的质量水平。 我不需要深入挖掘就能找到它们；这些是我在过去几个月里亲眼所见的事情。

因此，考虑到这些例子，旗舰系统框架几乎不可能构建一个至少在某一方面没有被破坏的应用程序，这一点也就不足为奇了。

特别是在苹果平台上，这种转变始于 2018 年左右，包括我已经提到过的那些“外星”应用程序。 正是在这个时候，Marzipan 项目（后来更名为 Catalyst）首次实现了 UIKit 代码在 Mac 上的重用。 技术评论家对结果进行了分析，这里有更多屏幕截图。

但苹果并没有做足功课，而是通过 SwiftUI 加强了跨平台开发的想法。 这个全新的、完全未经测试的框架只会带来更多性能、稳定性和视觉吸引力方面的问题。

我的结论是，降低质量标准是一种选择，而不是必然。 我拒绝接受这个选择。 这就是为什么即使七年后我仍然无法信任 SwiftUI。

概括

作为底线，并从一开始就回答这个问题，SwiftUI 到底出了什么问题？

如果你权衡其存在七年来尚未解决的所有问题，答案是，

一切。

或者至少是对于构建稳定、高性能和可维护系统来说重要的一切。

SwiftUI 的故事是一个平庸和标准下降的故事。 我们被要求用可预测的精度来换取便利的幻觉。 然后我们被迫要么花时间调试框架，要么按原样交付损坏的应用程序。

作为一名高级工程师，我发现这两种选择都没有吸引力。 我不尊重“行不行”的心态，我相信用户应该得到比“足够好”更好的东西。

SwiftUI 并不是真的很糟糕。 这是平庸的。 在我看来，这要糟糕得多。

所以目前，我仍然更喜欢“传统”UI 框架。

事后的想法

甚至在我开始这个频道之前，我就想到了写这篇文章的想法。 多年来，我一直在观察 SwiftUI 努力成为 AppKit 和 UIKit 的可靠替代品，换句话说，成为苹果在 2019 年所承诺的那样。

多年来，我一直在测试 SwiftUI 的新迭代，希望困扰它的问题最终能够得到解决。

但随着时间的推移，SwiftUI 并没有从根本上变得更好。 它和七年前一样半生不熟，使用 SwiftUI 构建的应用程序大多也同样不起眼。

但 SwiftUI 的挣扎并不是我观察到的唯一事情。 我也一直在观察软件工程师，他们真诚地相信，如果用 SwiftUI 构建的功能此时此刻就可以工作，那么他们的工作就完成了。 除非他们故意选择劣质工具，否则我并不会责怪他们。

好吧，也许有一点，因为你不能在不付出代价的情况下忽视长期的维护成本。

不管怎样，付钱的人通常不是个别工程师。他们的雇主是。 但在企业热衷于用人工智能代替人类的时代，很难指望他们的产品质量能够提高。 而且由于这些企业也将软件开发视为商品或线性生产，因此他们通常希望“快速”而不是“正确”地交付。 我们已经可以看到这种方法的结果，并且将来我们还会看到更多。
